When a football club sacks its manager, the next few matches often look better. Commentators call it the new manager bounce. The question is whether the sacking *caused* the improvement, or whether mean reversion was going to deliver it anyway.

## Association is not causation

Teams that fire their manager are not a random sample. They fire after a collapse. If you compare the five matches before a sacking to the five after, you will almost always see a bounce — and you will have learned nothing about the treatment. The interesting comparison is treated clubs versus similar clubs that were also in a slump but kept their manager.

## What's next

This post will use coarsened exact matching on 20 years of Big Five league data to estimate the average treatment effect on the treated. The notebook version — code, balance tables, and event-time plots — will replace this page. Until then, the question stands: after you match on pre-treatment form, is there anything left of the bounce?
